items.name: Internet Time Travel (danishv1)
items.what_it_does: Chrome MV3 extension, load-unpacked only (README: Web Store listing pending). You pick a date and it does three things. (1) Every page you open, including clicked Google results, is redirected to its Wayback Machine copy from that date (a declarativeNetRequest rule to web.archive.org/web/<date>/<url>). (2) Google searches get tbs=cdr:1,cd_max:<date>, which is Google's own custom date range. (3) YouTube stays live, but searches get before:<date>. The home feed, sidebar, end screens and comments are filtered, upload dates are shown relative to the chosen 'today', Shorts are hidden and the home feed is rebuilt from that era. You can mark sites as always live. It has no old-era Google or YouTube look, no music and no 'this year' rewriting. I read the README and the source files (content-google.js has the cd_max line, content-youtube.js the before: line, background.js the Wayback redirect). I did not run it.

result.verdict: No: nothing found does the whole thing in one product. That means picking a year, getting a Google that looks like that year and only returns results up to it, having links open as archived copies, YouTube limited to that year in its old look, a background player of that year's hits, all inside a Windows 95/98/XP style app. Parts do exist, almost all as tiny hobby projects from 2025 and 2026 with 0 to 300 users. Two exceptions are big, but each is narrower: Slop Evader and Pre-AI Search have about 10,000 users each, but only offer a fixed pre-ChatGPT cutoff. The closest to the 'no future' core is Internet Time Travel (GitHub danishv1, a Chrome extension loaded unpacked, one upload in August 2026, 0 stars). It caps Google with Google's own custom date range (tbs=cdr:1,cd_max), adds before: to YouTube searches and filters the feed, sidebar and comments, and sends every site you click to its Wayback copy from that date. I read its code but did not run it. Firefox's 'Time Machine (Google & YouTube)' also caps Google, but it has 1-star 'doesn't work' reviews. The closest to 'looks like that year' is Gplex Extended (Chrome Web Store, 316 users): Google's design for any year from 1997 to 2024, and YouTube through StarTube + V3. It deliberately shows today's results; I found no date filter in its code. On YouTube alone, bygone-yt (Greasy Fork, needs V3), Time Machine for YouTube (Firefox) and Optima Time Machine all limit videos to a year; bygone-yt also gives the old look. Throwback combines a 2008 Google look with 'Cached' links to 2008 Wayback copies, but the year is fixed. Music by year exists only as separate sites (The Nostalgia Machine, 88mph), connected to nothing. The retro desktop app does not exist. Frozen In Time OS describes almost exactly that (choose a year, a Windows VM from that era, 'TimeNet' with Wayback and an era search index), but by its own README it is a 13 KB launcher stub that doesn't start Windows or reach the Wayback Machine yet. Google Beta Browser (Electron, Windows 98 window, 1998 Google) is just a skin over DuckDuckGo with no date limit. Nobody rewrites 'this year' into the chosen year, and a date cap mostly makes that unnecessary, because a 2010 page that says 'this year' means 2010. Google itself ran a one-off 'search the January 2001 index' for its 10th birthday in 2008, long gone. Hard limits anyone building this will hit: Google's date filter relies on estimated page dates and lets newer pages through (several 2026 Slop Evader reviews). Many old results are dead links, so they need rewriting to Wayback copies, which only Internet Time Travel does, plus Throwback for 2008. The archive has essentially no Google results pages (my inference), so search has to be live Google with a date cap and page views have to come from the archive. Practical note for the owner: his 86Box Win95 + WebOne setup already covers part of the retro side. WebOne's config supports web.archive.org/web/<year>/ redirect rules and an ArchiveDateLimit, and WaybackProxy gives old browsers a web locked to one date. Bottom line: the idea is not 'already done'. Gplex Extended + Internet Time Travel + bygone-yt together would cover maybe 60 to 70 percent of the browser version today, but they are separate, fragile, low-user projects. The single integrated product (year look + date-capped results + archive links + YouTube + year music + retro shell) is still open.

result.verdict:
No. As of 2026-11-10 nothing combines the full idea: a year picker, real Google results locked to that year, 'this year' read as that year, Google and YouTube skins from that era, YouTube by year, that year's music player, and a Win95/98/XP shell. The pieces exist separately.

Closest for the search part: the Firefox add-on 'Time Machine (Google & YouTube)' (5/10). It applies any cutoff date to Google and YouTube and has a jump-to-Wayback button. But it is Firefox-only, has 8 users and a 1/5 rating, and its only review says it did not work.
- In Chrome, Pre-AI Search filters inside normal google.com: pre-2023 for free, any date only in the paid Pro tier.
- Slop Evader (Chrome) is fixed at 30 Nov 2022.

Closest for the retro-app part:
- win98.si and winxp.si: Win98/XP desktops whose Internet Explorer shows any site as archived in a year you pick.
- Desktop98: 1998 only, with Wayback IE, Winamp, and AI chat characters who never admit anything after 1998.
- TheOldNet: year dropdown for 1994-2010 plus an archive search.
None of these can run a real Google or YouTube search of that year.

Music by year is already solved: The Nostalgia Machine plays each year's hits from 1951 to 2025 through YouTube, with skip and back.

Nobody reads 'this year' as the chosen year, and my tests show it is the make-or-break piece:
- Brave with a strict 2005 range: 'music trends this year' returns nothing, while 'best songs 2005' returns only 2005 pages.
- YouTube with before:2010 plus 'this year': random old clips. Rewritten as 'music trends 2010': the real 2010 hits.

An era-accurate Google with real results is gone:
- oldgoogle.neocities.org shut down in December 2025.
- Google's own 2008 'search2001' index is a 404.
- elgoog's 1998 page always shows the same sample results.
- Google's 'Google in 1998' easter egg dates from 2013, not 2018, and its 2026 status is unverified.

'No future at all' cannot be guaranteed through Google, because its page dates are inferred and often wrong (HN examples show chatgpt.com pages dated 2010-2020). Only WaybackProxy enforces a hard limit (its DATE_TOLERANCE setting), and only for archived pages; WebOne's ArchiveDateLimit setting can do something similar in the owner's 86Box Windows 95.

Building blocks for his own version:
- Google's own date filter (the tbs=cdr URL parameter and the before: operator)
- YouTube's before:/after: operators
- Brave's custom date range, which was strict in my tests
- the Wayback Machine availability and CDX APIs
- Billboard year lists like The Nostalgia Machine's
- react-xp or 98.js as the retro desktop shell

Limits: Google launched in 1998 and YouTube in 2005. 'Me at the zoo', the first YouTube video, came up for before:2005-12-31, so there is no YouTube before 2005.

The idea is not already taken. What nobody has built is the combination of all these parts, plus reading 'this year' as the chosen year.

items.name: Time Machine (Google & YouTube)
items.what_it_does: Firefox-only add-on by Zaki Aslam (GitHub Zaki101Aslam/time-machine-firefox). You set a cutoff date. In 'Hide Newer' mode it rewrites every Google search URL to Google's own custom date range (tbs=cdr:1,cd_max:M/D/YYYY), so Google itself returns results from before the date. It also hides result cards whose snippet date, or any 4-digit year in the text, is newer, and it hides AI Overviews. On YouTube it only hides video cards whose 'N years ago' is newer than the cutoff, plus Shorts. It does not add before: to YouTube searches. It also works on DuckDuckGo and Bing. A popup button opens the current tab in the Wayback Machine at the cutoff date (current page only, not each result). No 'this year' rewriting, no period Google or YouTube look, no music, no Chrome version.

The README says it is 'pretty extremely incompleted', and Google CSE keys are being phased out, so only existing keys work.

result.verdict: The full combination does not exist as one product as of 2026-11-10. Nobody offers it end to end: pick any year 1998-2025, search in the real Google and get only results up to that year with 'this year' meaning that year, have Google and YouTube look like that year, limit YouTube to that year, add an optional period music player, and ship it as a Chrome extension or a Win95/98/XP-style app. The core mechanic is not new, though. It has been built several times in pieces, mostly in 2026. (1) Google itself shipped exactly this for one year in 2008 ('2001: A search odyssey': January 2001 index, 2001-style page, results linked to Internet Archive copies) and took it down after a month. (2) The closest living product working inside the regular Google and YouTube is the Firefox add-on 'Time Machine (Google & YouTube)' from Feb 2026. It takes a cutoff date, forces Google's own date range and hides newer YouTube cards. But it is Firefox-only (the owner uses Chrome), has about 8 users and a 1-star 'doesn't work' review, and has no period look, no music and no 'this year' rewrite. Rating 5/10. (3) The closest all-in-one feel is the self-hosted pair gs2009 + yt2009: 2009 Google look with an automatic before: date, result links sent to the Wayback Machine at a set date, and YouTube links sent to a 2009 YouTube frontend with its own date cutoff. But it is stuck on the 2009 look, needs Node servers plus SearXNG or an old Google CSE key and a YouTube API key, and has no music or OS shell. About 6/10 combined, 5/10 for gs2009 alone. (4) YouTube by year alone is solved many times: optima time machine (Chrome, unpacked, Oct 2026), bygone-yt, ChronoLock, RetroTube, dross.cc, and YouTube's own before: operator, which I tested today and which works. (5) Fixed-date versions are popular: Slop Evader and Pre-AI Search have about 10k users each, but lock to late 2022/2023, not a chosen year. (6) The retro app side exists without time-locked search. Reframe is a Windows .exe with IE5/Win98 and Netscape chrome and a Wayback year picker, but searches go to live DuckDuckGo. Others: oldweb.today, winxp.si, iRetro (iOS), TheOldNet, Protoweb. (7) Music by year is well covered: The Nostalgia Machine (1951-2025, YouTube, skip), Rewind, TapeDeck, Radiooooo. Not found anywhere: rewriting 'this year/latest/current' in the query to the chosen year; switching the real Google look per chosen year together with date-locked results for any year; one Chrome product that unifies Google + YouTube + music; and a strict 'no future' guarantee. A 2026 arXiv audit (2602.00758) found Google's before: filter still leaks post-cutoff pages for 71% of questions, and clicking a result opens today's live page unless it is routed through the Wayback Machine. Bottom line: the owner's idea is not 'already done'. Its parts exist, often as tiny, fresh 2026 projects, but the assembled, polished, year-selectable Google + YouTube + period-look + music experience does not, and the closest existing things score about 5-6/10. Ready-made design pieces for the retro look: Version Museum (23 years of Google Search design history), 98.css, XP.css and Webamp.

reports.result:
**Google date-lock feasibility (tested live 2026-11-10, 18:40 to 18:47 UTC)**

Tags: [LIVE] = tested in the Playwright browser today. [DOC: url] = I opened the page. [SEC] = search-result snippet or secondary source only. [U] = unverified.

## Bottom line
- **Date-locking real Google works mechanically.** `tbs=cdr` and `before:` apply the same cap on Google's own estimated page date. Across 6 results pages, all 49 snippet dates shown were 2010 or earlier. [LIVE]
- **It does not keep the future out.** On literal queries, 18 of 40 first-page results were clearly modern pages, and 4 more were likely modern. The leaks were live homepages, store and category pages carrying an old "first seen" date, undated social/Q&A cards, and one paper bylined 2012. [LIVE]
- **Rewriting the query helps most.**
  - "best phone" had 6/10 modern results. "best phone 2010" had 0/9.
  - "music trends this year" had 1/10 results about 2010. "music trends 2010" had 6/10. [LIVE]
- **New obstacle since Aug 2026:** result links are now `google.com/goto?url=CAES...`, an opaque token. The real URL is not anywhere in the page. [LIVE] + [DOC: https://serpapi.com/blog/googles-new-goto-redirect-urls-resolution-in-progress/]
- **Chrome extension:** run a content script on the results page the user loads, and use declarativeNetRequest (DNR) to add the URL parameters. Do not fetch Google in the background.
- **Standalone app:** Google's search API is closed to new customers. Use the Brave or Exa APIs. Add Wayback CDX as the "did this page exist by year Y" check, and use it to open period snapshots.

## 1. Mechanisms

**Custom date range (`tbs=cdr`)**
- Format: `&tbs=cdr:1,cd_min:1/1/1995,cd_max:12/31/2010` (M/D/YYYY). Works with `hl=en`. [LIVE]
- Date order with `hl=de` or `hl=ru` is [U]. Test it before relying on it.

**`before:` / `after:` operators**
- `before:2011-01-01` gives the same filter with slightly different ranking. Overlap with `tbs=cdr` was 6/10 and 9/10, with identical displayed dates. [LIVE]
- The operator stays visible in the query and the page title, which hurts immersion. `tbs` keeps the search box clean. [LIVE]
- Danny Sullivan said in May 2025 it is "still in beta" and that "it can be difficult for us to know the exact date of a document". [DOC: https://www.seroundtable.com/google-before-and-after-operators-still-in-beta-39361.html]
- The year-only form `before:2011` is documented. [SEC: searchengineland.com/?p=315184]

**`tbs=qdr:h|d|w|m|y` (optionally with a number)**
- This is relative to now, so it cannot express "before 2010". Not usable here. [SEC]

**`udm=14` (the "Web" tab)**
- Shows links only ("Web results"), no AI Overview, and combines fine with `tbs=cdr`. [LIVE]
- Launched May 2024. [SEC]
- `tbm` and `udm` cannot be combined. [DOC: https://serpapi.com/search-api]
- One test on the All tab with a date filter showed no AI Overview, but an Images block appeared and I did not date-check it. [LIVE, one query only]

**How Google decides a page's date**
- It estimates a "byline date" from several signals: a prominent visible date and schema.org `datePublished` / `dateModified`. No single factor is used and nothing is guaranteed. [DOC: https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/publication-dates]
- Observed: homepages and evergreen pages keep an early date while serving 2026 content:
  - verizon.com: "Feb 11, 2008", snippet says "First to 5G"
  - android.com: "Mar 25, 2010", snippet lists "Google Pixel 11 Pro ... $1,299.00"
  - trends.google.com: "Sep 13, 2006"
- music.apple.com/search was dated "Nov 6, 2009", but Wayback's first capture of music.apple.com is 2018-12-27. [LIVE + CDX]
- So the filter means "Google thinks this URL existed by then". It does not mean "the content is as of then".

**JavaScript requirement**
- Google requires JavaScript since Jan 2025. [SEC]
- The first navigation in this session returned 200, then a JavaScript reload with `&sei=...`. [LIVE, network log]
- Google responses carry `X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN`, so a web app cannot iframe Google. [LIVE]

## 2. Live leak test
**Setup:** Playwright Chromium, logged out, German IP, `hl=en&gl=us`, first page only. 8 requests in about 7 minutes, 26 to 180 seconds apart. No captcha and no consent wall appeared.

**The browser was not exclusive.** Another agent navigated my tab to patreon.com/re_aol before I could read request #2, so that result was lost. After that I used throwaway pages that I closed after each call. Both tabs that were open when I started are gone now, and I did not close them. One is left, showing about:blank.

|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | "music trends this year", `tbs=cdr` max 12/31/2010, `udm=14` | 3 sure + 2 likely / 10 | Apple Music "Nov 6, 2009"; live trends.google.com; ScienceDirect paper "by P Maymin · 2012"; current Wikipedia article dated 2004; Lumen Learning dated 2007 |
| 2 | lost (tab hijacked) | | |
| 3 | "music trends this year before:2011-01-01", `udm=14` | 3 sure + 2 likely / 10 | Same Apple Music and Google Trends; undated "Radial by The Orchard" card naming the "27th Annual Latin GRAMMY" (2026) |
| 4 | "best phone", `tbs=cdr`, `udm=14` | 6 / 10 | android.com (Pixel 11); verizon.com (5G); bestbuy.com "May 27, 2010" mentioning Google Pixel; live Consumer Reports ratings page; buy.gazelle.com store; undated "630+ views" card naming Gabb/Troomi |
| 5 | "best phone before:2011-01-01", `udm=14` | 6 / 10 | Same set as #4 |

**Background fetch from the service worker: possible, but don't**
- Host permissions allow cross-origin fetch. [DOC: https://developer.chrome.com/docs/extensions/develop/concepts/network-requests]
- Requests are treated as same-site, so Google cookies are sent, except when the user blocks third-party cookies. [DOC: https://developer.chrome.com/docs/extensions/develop/concepts/storage-and-cookies]
- With cookies, a same-origin fetch got full results HTML (test #8). I did not test a real service worker. [U]
- Problems:
  - Service workers have no DOMParser; parsing needs an offscreen document with reason `DOM_PARSER`. [DOC: https://developer.chrome.com/docs/extensions/reference/api/offscreen]
  - Without cookies you hit the JavaScript bounce.
  - Background queries count as automated traffic and lead to the `/sorry` captcha. [SEC: support.google.com/websearch/answer/86640]

## 4. Query rewriting
Verified effect: tests #6 and #7.

- **Relative years:**
  - "this year" / "current year" -> Y
  - "last year" / "previous year" -> Y-1
  - "next year" -> Y+1 (predictions written in Y)
  - "N years ago" -> Y-N
- **Present-time words** ("now", "today", "currently", "nowadays", "these days", "right now"): drop them and append Y.
  - Alternative for "today": use the month and year (e.g. "November 2010") and set `cd_max` to the same calendar day in Y.
- **Explicit years after Y** (e.g. "2026"): replace with Y, or show "this year hasn't happened yet". Keep years up to Y unchanged.
- **No year in the query** but words like best, top, new, latest, trend(s), news, popular, price, review(s), hits: append Y. This was the single biggest quality lever.
- Do not touch quoted phrases or `site:`, `before:` or `after:`.
- **Russian and German:**
  - "в этом году" / "dieses Jahr" -> Y
  - "в прошлом году" / "letztes Jahr" -> Y-1
  - "сейчас", "сегодня", "aktuell", "heute", "neueste" -> append Y
  - JavaScript's `\b` is ASCII-only, so use `(?<!\p{L})...(?!\p{L})` with the `u` flag for Cyrillic.
- **Untested idea:** for "this year / now / latest" intent, also set `cd_min:1/1/Y`.

## Recommended approach

**(a) Chrome extension (MV3)**
1. **Year picker** in the popup, stored locally.
2. **Add the parameters with DNR:** a dynamic rule on `www.google.com/search` (main frame) with `queryTransform.addOrReplaceParams` setting `tbs=cdr:1,cd_min:1/1/1990,cd_max:12/31/Y`. [DOC: https://developer.chrome.com/docs/extensions/reference/api/declarativeNetRequest]

   - Check for redirect loops. [U]
3. **Rewrite the query** in a content script when the user submits.
   - Searches typed in the address bar skip that script, so re-navigate them with `location.replace`.
   - Put the user's original text back into the search box afterwards.
4. **Filter cards in a content script on the results page.** Hide:
   - cards with no date and no byline year
   - byline year later than Y
   - a year later than Y in the title or snippet, or a curated list of anachronisms (Pixel, 5G, Gemini, TikTok and so on)
   - a bare-domain `cite` (homepage)

5. **When the user clicks a result**, a DNR redirect sends navigations started from google.com (excluding google and archive.org domains) to an extension page. That page must be listed in `web_accessible_resources`. It runs the CDX lookup and opens `web.archive.org/web/<timestamp at or before Y>/<url>`, or shows "this page does not exist yet in Y". This sidesteps the opaque `/goto` links, the modern content and the "never later" problem. This is a design only and untested. Links and resources inside a Wayback page may resolve to later captures. [U]
6. **Stop on `/sorry`** and tell the user. Never search Google in the background.

# Wayback Machine as "the web of year Y": research results

**Budget:** 56 requests to archive.org, spaced at least 3.5 s apart. No 429s. Failures happened only on heavy queries: 2× 504 (the gateway gives up at 60 s), 1× 503 "Temporarily Offline" page, 1× stream cut at 90 s, and 1× transient TCP refusal that worked on retry.

## Summary
- **Resolver:** use CDX `to=<Y>1231235959&filter=statuscode:200&limit=-1&fastLatest=true`. It answers in 0.7 to 1.6 s. Then open that exact 14-digit timestamp, which is served with no redirect. VERIFIED
- **Wayback "closest" leaks the future everywhere:** in the Availability API, in year-only URLs, in links inside archived pages, and in the archived Google search box. I captured 5 concrete forward jumps. VERIFIED
- **Year-only URLs:** `/web/2010/<url>` is padded to the END of 2010, so it landed on 2011-01-01 00:14. VERIFIED
- **Display mode:** `if_` hides the toolbar but keeps links rewritten. Links inside an `if_` page drop the `if_` flag, so the toolbar comes back after one click unless the extension forces `if_` again. VERIFIED
- **CDX rate limit:** the hard limit in 2026 is 30 requests/min per IP, and the library guidance is 24/min. Ignoring 429s gets the IP blocked at the firewall for 1 hour, and the block doubles each time after that. Verified only from secondary sources (quotes below).
- **Year tables:** Google 1998-2025 and YouTube 2005-2025 are complete. Archived Google results pages were found for 2000 and for 2011-2025. **2001-2010 has no results pages**, so I list a substitute.

## 1. CDX: latest 200 capture at or before the cutoff

```
https://web.archive.org/cdx/search/cdx?url=<URL>&to=<YYYY>1231235959&filter=statuscode:200&limit=-1&fastLatest=true&output=json&fl=timestamp,original,statuscode,mimetype
```
- **Hit:** `[["timestamp",...],["20101231191441","http://www.google.com/","200","text/html"]]`. VERIFIED
- **No capture:** `[]` with HTTP 200 (tested youtube.com, cutoff 2004). VERIFIED
- **Then open** `https://web.archive.org/web/<exact ts>if_/<original>`. All 24 exact-timestamp fetches returned 200 with no redirect. VERIFIED
- **`limit=-1`** returns the last line, because results are in ascending time order. VERIFIED
- **`fastLatest=true`** gives the same answer faster: 0.94 s with it, 1.58 s without (google.com, one sample). VERIFIED

- **IA staff in 2023** (Slack, quoted in edgi/wayback issue #137):
  - CDX: "limited to an average of 60/min".
  - "If 429s are ignored for more than a minute we block the IP at the firewall (no connection) for 1 hour."
  - "Subsequent 429s ... double that time."
  - Limits are measured over 5-minute windows. Timemap 100/min, archived pages 600/min. IA asked clients to default to 80% of these.
  - VERIFIED as published quotes. Not an official IA page.
- **2026 update** (edgi `wayback` library):
  - v0.5.1 (2026-06-19) lowered the CDX default to 24/min "to match the actual hard limits now set on Wayback Machine servers". The code is `0.8*30/60`, so the hard limit is 30/min.
  - Timemap now shares the CDX limit.
  - v0.5.0 (2026-05-22) stopped retrying on 429 automatically, to avoid IP blocks.
  - VERIFIED from the library docs and source.
- **Official CDX README:** says nothing about rate limits and recommends the Pagination API for bulk queries. VERIFIED
- **"15 requests/min" community reports:** UNVERIFIED.
- **Availability API limit:** not documented. Treat it like CDX.
- **What it means:** each user's IP gets about 24 lookups/min. That is enough to resolve on each click, but not to resolve every image or script on a page.

### Chrome MV3 design (cutoff C = `<Y>1231235959`)
1. **Search result click.** Run the CDX query from section 1, then `location.replace` to the exact timestamp with `if_`.
   - If CDX returns `[]`, show an era-style "The page cannot be displayed" page.
   - Optional: pre-check a whole results page with one Availability batch POST. Keep items whose timestamp is at or before C; resolve the rest with CDX on click.
2. **Every later navigation:** links inside pages, back/forward, typed URLs.
   - **Main rule:** a DNR dynamic rule with an RE2 regex rebuilt for each selected year, applied to `main_frame`:
     `^https?://web\.archive\.org/web/(FUTURE\d{0,10})([a-z]{2}_)?/(.*)$`
     It redirects with `regexSubstitution` to `chrome-extension://<id>/resolve.html#\3`, which must be a web-accessible resource. The resolver page runs CDX with `to=C`.
   - **Safety net:** `webRequest.onBeforeRedirect` (watch-only in MV3, gives `redirectUrl`) or `onHeadersReceived` (`location`, `x-archive-redirect-reason`). If the timestamp is after C, call `chrome.tabs.update(tabId,{url:resolver})`.
   - Neither of these is tested: whether DNR rules match the target of a server 302 isn't documented, and whether `regexSubstitution` can redirect to a `chrome-extension://` URL is unconfirmed. Both need a prototype test.
   - **Force no toolbar:** rewrite `main_frame` `^https://web\.archive\.org/web/(\d{14})/(.*)` to `.../web/\1if_/\2`. The rewritten URL no longer matches, so there is no loop.
   - **Images, scripts, styles, fonts, media, XHR and sub-frames with a future timestamp:** `block` them, which looks like an era-authentic broken image. Do not resolve them through CDX, because of the per-IP limit.
   - **Live-web leak:** block requests with `initiatorDomains:["web.archive.org"]` and `excludedRequestDomains:["archive.org"]`. This still allows `web-static.archive.org`.
   - **Archived Google search box and Wayback calendar URLs:** catch `/web/*/http(s)://www.google.*/search?` and `*` calendar URLs, and send them to the time machine's own results page.
   - **DNR limits** (VERIFIED, Chrome docs): RE2 syntax; each rule under 2 KB once compiled; at most 1000 regex rules; 30,000 safe dynamic rules, 5,000 unsafe dynamic rules (redirects count as unsafe); `updateDynamicRules` is atomic. Blocking `webRequest` in MV3 is available only to policy-installed extensions.

## 3. Music by year

**US charts (Billboard year-end lists on Wikipedia)**
- The title "Billboard Year-End Hot 100 singles of YEAR" works for every year 1946-2025 when redirects are followed [T]:
  - 1946-48 redirect to "top singles".
  - 1949-55 redirect to "top 30".
  - 1956-58 redirect to "top 50".
  - 1959-2025 are direct pages.
- Fetch URL, then take the first `table.wikitable` [T]:
  `https://en.wikipedia.org/w/api.php?action=parse&page=Billboard_Year-End_Hot_100_singles_of_2010&prop=text&format=json&formatversion=2&redirects=1`
- Columns are `No. | Title | Artist(s)` [T]:
  - The first header is "№" instead of "No." in 1962, 1986, 1992-94, 1996, 1998 and 2007.
  - 1946-48 use "No. (Rank)" with values like "35 (41)".
  - Titles are wrapped in quotes and link to the song's article.
- Row counts [T]: 1946=41, 1947=47, 1948=39; 1949-55=30; 1956-57=50; 1958=51; 1959-2025=100, except 1969=101 (tie at #100).
- Parsing trap [T]: when one artist has consecutive ranks, the Artist cell spans several rows (2016 Bieber #1-2, 2024 SZA #19-20). Tied ranks behave the same way. You must expand these spans or the columns shift.
- Rate limit [T]: a quick burst of requests got HTTP 429. With a descriptive User-Agent and 2-3 seconds between calls, all 80 years loaded fine.
- **Already scraped:** all 80 years, 7,189 rows, no empty cells. File and scraper are listed at the end.

**Other countries**
- **UK, every year:** "List of UK top-ten singles in YEAR" exists for 1952-2025 [T].
  - Main table: `Entered (week ending) | Weeks in top 10 | Single | Artist | Peak | Peak reached (week ending) | Weeks at peak`.
  - Includes divider rows like "Singles in 2009" for carry-overs. Checked on 1985, 2010 and 2024 [T].
- **UK, year-end with sales:** "YEAR in British music charts" exists for 1999-2018 [T]. The 2010 page has a top-50 table `No. | Title | Artist | Peak position | Sales` [T].
- **Germany:** "Liste der Nummer-eins-Hits in Deutschland (YEAR)" on German Wikipedia exists for 1954-2025 [T, existence only].

**Getting YouTube video IDs without a search**
- Route: song article, then its Wikidata item, then property P1651 "YouTube video ID" [T].
- Share of Billboard year-end songs with at least one ID [T]: 1965 8/100, 1985 35, 2000 50, 2010 80, 2020 81, 2025 25.
- Deezer, Spotify and Apple Music ID properties cover at most 8 songs per 100 [T], so they are not useful.

**Playback options**
- **YouTube:**
  - Embedding by search term (`listType: 'search'`) stopped working on 15 Nov 2020 [V], so you need real video IDs.
  - The search API (search.list) is now documented as "Quota impact: 100 calls per day", costing 1 unit in a separate "Search Queries" bucket [V, doc text as of today]. It supports `publishedBefore`/`publishedAfter` and `videoEmbeddable=true` [V].
  - [rec] Look IDs up only when needed, cache them permanently, and pre-fill from Wikidata first.
  - YouTube's minimum-functionality rules [V]:
    - The page must send an HTTP Referer header; without it the player shows "Error 153" [V2].
    - The player must be at least 200x200.
    - Nothing may overlay or obscure the player.
    - The player may not be modified.
  - So a hidden or Winamp-skinned YouTube audio player breaks the rules.
- **Deezer** [T]:
  - `https://api.deezer.com/search?q=<artist> <title>` returns a 30-second MP3 in `data[].preview`, no key needed.
  - Strict field search returned 0 hits for Kesha's "Tik Tok" (Deezer spells it "TiK ToK"). Use plain search plus fuzzy matching.
  - Preview links are signed and expired about 15 minutes after I got them. Fetch right before playing.
  - No CORS permission header was returned for an extension origin, so call it from the background service worker or offscreen document with host permissions.
  - The first hit can be a remix; prefer a non-remix album and a duration close to the original.
  - Terms: non-commercial use only [V].
- **iTunes Search API** [T]:
  - `https://itunes.apple.com/search?term=...&entity=song&country=US` returns a 30-second `.m4a` preview and artwork. CORS is open (`*`). Limit is about 20 calls per minute [V].
  - Terms [V]: previews are for promotion only, must sit next to a "Download on iTunes" badge, need attribution, may only be streamed (not cached), and may not be used "for independent entertainment value". A background radio conflicts with this.
- **Match test on each year's top 25** [T]: Deezer and iTunes each found 24/25 (1959), 25/25 (1975), 24/25 (1995), 25/25 (2015).
  - Misses: the double A-side "Boombastic" / "In the Summertime" (split titles on " / ") and the artist alias "Dave 'Baby' Cortez".
- **Spotify** [V]: skip it.
  - The Web Playback SDK needs Premium and may not be used commercially without approval.
  - Development mode allows at most 5 users, and the app owner must have Premium.
  - Higher quotas are only for organizations with at least 250k monthly users (since May 15, 2025).
  - Apps created after Nov 27, 2024 lost 30-second previews in bulk track responses, recommendations and audio features.
  - One community post says playback never connects in development mode after the Feb/Mar 2026 changes [U].

**MV3 notes**
- **Extension pages** [V]: the default security policy is `script-src 'self'; object-src 'self';` with a minimum of `script-src 'self' 'wasm-unsafe-eval'; object-src 'self';`. You cannot add `'unsafe-eval'` or remote script hosts. Bundle all JavaScript locally (no unpkg links). CSS-only kits are fine.
- **google.com/search** [T]: its security header today only covers object, base and script sources. Nothing restricts styles or fonts, so injected CSS and extension fonts load.
- **Fonts in content-script CSS:**
  - Reference them as `url('chrome-extension://__MSG_@@extension_id__/fonts/x.woff2')` [V].
  - List them in `web_accessible_resources` with `matches: ["https://www.google.com/*"]`; only the origin part of the pattern is used [V].
  - Content scripts themselves do not need to be listed [V].
- **youtube.com** [T]: sends `require-trusted-types-for 'script'`. Avoid `innerHTML` in injected UI and build nodes directly. Whether this affects extension scripts is [U].
- **Background music:**
  - An offscreen document for audio closes after 30 seconds of silence, only one is allowed, and it cannot be focused [V].
  - The Side Panel (Chrome 114+, `open()` from 116+ and only after a user action) stays open across tabs when set globally [V]. It suits a persistent player.

critique:
## 1. Landscape (deduped, closest to a Chrome v1 first)

- **Internet Time Travel** (github.com/danishv1/internet-time-travel, Chrome MV3, load unpacked)
  - Does: caps Google with `tbs=cdr`, adds `before:` to YouTube and filters its feed, sidebar and comments, and redirects every opened page to Wayback at the chosen date.
  - Missing: no era look, no music, no "this year" rewrite.
  - My check: the repo exists, MIT license, created and last pushed 2026-08-07, 0 stars. Nobody has run it.
- **Time Machine (Google & YouTube)**: Firefox only. Caps Google and hides newer cards. On YouTube it only hides cards, no `before:`. 8 users, a 1-star "doesn't work" review.
- **gs2009 + yt2009** (self-hosted Node)
  - gs2009: 2009 Google look, adds `before:` automatically, links results to Wayback. It needs SearXNG, because Google's Custom Search API takes no new keys and ends 2027-01-01. Only one report found it, and nobody ran it.
  - yt2009: 2009 YouTube with `only_old` and `adaptive_old` (I checked the flags file).
- **Gplex Extended** (Chrome Web Store, 316 users; MIT userscript fork Ziptino9098/Gplex-Fixed)
  - Gives Google's look for any year 1997-2024, results pages included. YouTube's look comes through StarTube + V3.
  - Shows today's results, no date cap.
- **YouTube-only date locks:** bygone-yt (needs closed-source V3, buggy), Optima Time Machine (Chrome, unpacked), Time Machine for YouTube, ChronoLock, RetroTube (Firefox), dross.cc, timemachinevideos.com. YouTube's own `before:` works; three reports tested it.
- **Fixed-cutoff Google:**
  - Pre-AI Search: 10k users. Free tier is pre-2023 only; any date needs the paid Pro tier.
  - Slop Evader: fixed at 2022-11-30, works from a popup only.
- **Fixed-era looks:** Throwback (Chrome: 2008 Google with 2008 Wayback "Cached" links, 2009 YouTube), Google 2008 Retro, Old Google 2014, CustomTube, YouTube Redux.
- **Retro shells with Wayback by year, but no real search:**
  - Reframe: Windows .exe, year picker, search goes to live DuckDuckGo.
  - Others: win98.si / winxp.si, Desktop98 (1998 only), TheOldNet (1994-2010), oldweb.today, 98.js.org, react-xp.
  - Proxies: WaybackProxy, and WebOne (already in the owner's 86Box).
- **Music by year:** The Nostalgia Machine (1951-2025, YouTube, skip/back), Rewind, TapeDeck, Radiooooo (decades only), Playback.fm, 88mph.
- **Dead precedents:**
  - Google's own search2001: the January 2001 index with 2001 look and Wayback result links, online Sep-Oct 2008 only.
  - oldgoogle.neocities.org: closed December 2025.
  - yttm.tv, Search a Year, Memento.

**Verdict:** the full idea does not exist as one product. The core trick is not new: Google did a one-year version in 2008, and every tool automates `tbs=cdr` and YouTube's `before:`. What nobody has built yet:
- rewriting "this year" to the chosen year
- strict no-future browsing (every Wayback-based tool uses the "closest" lookup)
- the matching year's look on top of capped results
- a music player for the chosen year
- all of it in one Chrome extension or app

If the checks below pass, the best Chrome base is Internet Time Travel plus Gplex Extended.

**Unverified but high-impact:**
- How Internet Time Travel actually behaves. Its Wayback mode uses `/web/<date>/<url>`, which the Wayback report showed jumps forward in time, so it is not strict.
- Pre-AI Search Pro: if its custom range takes any year and stays on inside google.com, the Google cap already exists in Chrome as a paid product.
- Gplex Extended combined with a date cap: never tried. Also unknown whether the store build has the same MIT license as the fork.
- Reframe: only one report, not run, license unchecked. It is the best base for the desktop-app route.
- V3/Vorapis in Chrome: no Chrome Web Store release, and reviews from October and November 2026 report errors. bygone-yt and StarTube both depend on it.
- The `/goto` result links: only one report saw them, in a logged-out test.

## 2. Contradictions

- **"This year" rewriting.**
  - Stores/GitHub report: mostly unnecessary under a date cap (reasoning only).
  - Three other reports tested it live (Web/communities, YouTube, Google date filter):
    - Google: 1/10 results on topic, against 6/10 with "2010" in the query.
    - Brave: nothing at all, while "best songs 2005" returned real 2005 pages.
    - YouTube: random old clips, against the real 2010 hits after rewriting.
  - Evidence supports the live tests. Rewriting is required.
- **Closest product.**
  - Web/communities and skeptic reports: the Firefox add-on.
  - Stores/GitHub report: Internet Time Travel.
  - The Stores/GitHub report is right for a Chrome user. I confirmed the repo exists, but nobody has run it.
- **"Strict no future" claims for Wayback-based tools** (Internet Time Travel, Desktop98, winxp.si, Reframe, iRetro, TheOldNet, Protoweb, oldweb.today).
  - The Wayback report captured five forward redirects. For example, `/web/2010/` landed on 2011-01-01.
  - Evidence supports the Wayback report. Only a CDX lookup with `to=<Y>1231235959`, then opening that exact timestamp, is strict.
  - WaybackProxy (one report calls it the only real switch, another says it leaks): I checked. `DATE_TOLERANCE` defaults to 365 days, and the README lists newer pages as a known issue. It is strict only when set to 0, which nobody tested.
- **yt2009 date filter.**
  - The Stores/GitHub report found none in the README; the skeptic report found `only_old`. The skeptic report is right: `yt2009_flags.htm` has `only_old` and `adaptive_old`.
  - On the API key the Stores/GitHub report is right: the README calls it "highly recommended", not required. License is Apache-2.0.
- **Archived Google results pages, 2001-2010.**
  - The Wayback report found none; the era-design report cites one from November 2002. The era-design report is right: CDX returns `20021105033451` for `google.com/search?q=linux`, status 200.
  - So the real gap is 2001 and 2003-2010.
  - Also: the Wayback report's 1998 homepage (`19981111184551`) is a 212-byte stub. Use `19981202230410` instead.
- **Maintained old YouTube looks for 2005-2012.**
  - The YouTube report says there are none. Stores/GitHub and skeptic reports name yt2009 (pushed 2026-11-09) and StarTube (pushed 2026-07-09).
  - Those two reports have the facts right. In practice the YouTube report has a point: yt2009 is a server, and StarTube needs V3, so neither drops into a Chrome extension.
- **Era Google look has to be built by hand** (the era-design plan). Gplex Extended already covers 1997-2024. Evaluate it first.
- **The Chrome Web Store would reject a Google look** (the era-design report's prediction). Gplex Extended and Throwback are both live there. So such listings pass today, though a takedown stays possible. This does not matter for an unpacked personal extension.
- **What date Google filters on.**
  - Web/communities report: "last updated before", so updated pages drop out.
  - Google date-filter report, live: verizon.com dated 2008 shows 5G, and android.com dated 2010 shows the Pixel 11.
  - The live test is right. The cap uses an early estimated date, so updated pages stay in. That is the main source of leaks.
- **Design conflict between two reports.**
  - The Google date-filter report checks every result's domain against the Wayback index (CDX), up to 10 calls per results page.
  - The Wayback report measured a budget of about 24 CDX calls per minute per IP. Ignoring the 429 errors gets the IP blocked for an hour, doubling each time.
  - Fix: look a result up only when it is clicked, and cache by domain.
- **Minor:**
  - Slop Evader dropped DuckDuckGo: the Web/communities report is right.
  - Old'aVista does have a year filter, partly broken: the Web/communities report is right.
  - Memento's backend is dead.

## 3. Open questions for v1, each with the one check that settles it

**Google cap**
- Does a declarativeNetRequest rule adding `tbs=cdr` loop with Google's `&sei=` reload, and what date order does it need under German or Russian settings? Check: a one-rule test extension in the owner's logged-in Chrome, searching in English, German and Russian. Look at the "Custom range" chip and record the date strings for the parser.
- Does the owner's Chrome get the opaque `/goto` links? Check: inspect one result link.
- How much leaks after card filtering, and how many good undated results get hidden? Check: 10 rewritten queries at 2005 and 2010.
- Leaks outside the result cards: knowledge panel, "People also ask", top stories, autocomplete, doodle. Check: search an entity such as "justin bieber" capped at 2010.
- Are there enough results for 1998-2003? Check: 3 queries capped at 1999 and at 2002.

**"This year" rewriting**
- The rules have only been tested on 2 query pairs, and Russian/German rules are untested. Check: a set of 20 queries, compared before and after.
- Searches typed in the address bar: reload the page with the rewritten query (`location.replace`) or rewrite it with a redirect rule, and does Google's box keep showing the original text? Check: build both on 3 queries.

**Wayback with no future**
- Does a redirect rule catch the destination after Google's `/goto` redirect and send it to `chrome-extension://<id>/resolve.html#<url>`? Check: a one-rule prototype, then click 3 results.
- Does the rule catch Wayback's own forward redirects? Check: open `/web/20041231235959/http://www.youtube.com/`; the result must not be a 2005 capture.
- How many results have no capture by the chosen year (dead clicks)? Check: CDX lookups with `to=Y` for 50 results, kept under 20 per minute, timing each click.

**YouTube**
- Searches made inside YouTube's page go through a POST request (`/youtubei/v1/search`) that redirect rules cannot change. Check: run Internet Time Travel's `content-youtube.js`; all results must be in or before the year, with no `before:` showing in the box.
- Is `before:` inclusive, and in which timezone? Check: a known December 31 upload, searched with `before:Y-12-31` and with `before:(Y+1)-01-01`.
- Can a content script write HTML on youtube.com (Trusted Types)? Check: set `innerHTML` from a content script.
- Which code can be reused: Optima, bygone-yt, StarTube? Check: their license files.
- Do V3, StarTube and bygone-yt work in Chrome today? Check: Tampermonkey in a test profile.

**Era looks**
- Does Gplex Extended keep the date cap and draw the filtered results in the year's look? Check: test profile, pick 2005, open a `tbs=cdr` URL.

**Music**
- Does the player play in the owner's real Chrome side panel (headless: 3 of 4 tracks failed), start after the year click, and keep playing across tabs? Check: load the `extD` test extension and queue 20 songs from the 2010 list.
- Where do the rest of the YouTube video IDs come from? Wikidata has them for between 8 and 81 of each year's 100 songs. Does The Nostalgia Machine's `years.min.js` already hold IDs, and under which license? Check: search the file for YouTube IDs and read the repo's LICENSE.

## 4. Risks the reports missed

- **the owner's own browsing.**
  - What breaks: a global rule caps every search he makes, and redirects send his work browsing to Wayback. His YouTube history also fills with 2005 videos, and redirect rules from other extensions conflict.
  - Fix: a separate Chrome profile, a visible year badge and an off switch. Redirect only links opened from capped results.
- **IP reputation.** Today's tests already sent about 250 YouTube requests, 56 archive.org requests and some Google requests from his home IP, and one test hit a Google captcha. Pause automated testing from that IP, and never resolve `/goto` links ahead of a click.
- **Google page changes.** Class names are scrambled, `/goto` arrived in August 2026, and logged-in, A/B-tested and localized pages differ. Add a self-test that shows "filter broken" instead of leaking silently. Only one part of the extension should redraw the results page.
- **archive.org.**
  - It returned 503/504 errors during today's tests, and the Wayback Machine was down for days in October 2024 (my own knowledge).
  - Fallback: an era-style "Cannot find server" page, never the live page.
  - An empty availability answer means "unknown", not "did not exist".
- **YouTube embeds.**
  - Some videos won't play in the embed: region blocks on a German IP, age limits, embedding switched off. Skip these automatically.
  - Send the extension's own address as the Referer, not example.com.
  - The player must stay visible, at least 200x200 and uncovered. A Winamp look can frame it but not hide it.
- **Legal and naming.**
  - Keep "Google", "YouTube", "Time Machine" (Apple's backup feature, probably a registered mark) and "Wayback Machine" out of any public name.
  - V3 is closed source and cannot be bundled.
  - The 98.css font is CC BY-SA. Wikipedia's chart lists are CC BY-SA, and Billboard and EU database rights matter only if this is published.
  - Scraping YouTube without an API key breaks YouTube's terms.
- **Performance.**
  - Each click costs a CDX lookup of 0.7 to 1.6 s, then archived HTML that takes 6.2 s on average and up to 23 s. Show an era-style "Opening page" screen.
  - Gplex Extended injects a 9 MB script into every Google page.
